content: A joint is the anatomical location where two or more bones come into contact. Joints are designed to facilitate movement and provide mechanical support to the body. They are categorized based on their structural and functional characteristics. Structural Classification of Joints: 1. Fibrous Joints (Immovable Joints): These joints are connected by dense connective tissue, primarily composed of collagen. They are further divided into three subtypes: Sutures: Found between the bones of the skull. In fetal skulls, sutures are wide to allow slight movement during childbirth, but they later become rigid and immovable (synarthrodial). Syndesmoses: These are located between long bones, such as the radius and ulna in the forearm or the tibia and fibula in the leg. Unlike other fibrous joints, syndesmoses allow limited movement (amphiarthrodial), though not as much as synovial joints. Gomphoses: These are specialized joints between the roots of teeth and the sockets in the maxilla or mandible. 2. Cartilaginous Joints: These joints are entirely connected by cartilage and allow more movement than fibrous joints but less than synovial joints. Examples include the joint between the manubrium and the sternum, as well as the intervertebral discs. Primary Cartilaginous Joints (Synchondroses): These are formed by hyaline cartilage or fibrocartilage, often found between ossification centers. They may ossify with age. Examples include the joint between the first rib and the manubrium of the sternum, as well as growth plates in long bones. These joints typically allow no movement or minimal movement. Secondary Cartilaginous Joints (Symphyses): These are fibrocartilaginous joints, usually located in the midline of the body. Examples include the intervertebral discs and the pubic symphysis. These joints allow limited movement. 3. Synovial Joints: Synovial joints are characterized by a space between the articulating bones, which is filled with synovial fluid. These joints are the most mobile of all joint types and include examples such as the knee and shoulder. Synovial joints are further classified into: Ball and socket joints (e.g., shoulder, hip) Condyloid joints (e.g., wrist between radius and carpals) Saddle joints (e.g., joint between carpal and metacarpal of the thumb) Hinge joints (e.g., elbow) Pivot joints (e.g., radius and ulna) Gliding joints (e.g., between carpals) Functional Classification of Joints: 1. Synarthrosis (Immovable Joints): These joints allow little to no movement. Most synarthroses are fibrous joints. Synchondroses: Joints where bones are connected by cartilage. Synostoses: Joints where two initially separate bones fuse into one. For example, the plates of the cranium fuse as a child grows. Premature fusion of these plates can lead to craniostenosis, a condition that may cause skull deformities and brain damage due to restricted growth of the skull. 2. Amphiarthrosis (Slightly Movable Joints): These joints allow limited movement. The articulating bone surfaces are covered with hyaline cartilage and joined by fibrocartilage. Most amphiarthroses are cartilaginous joints. 3. Diarthrosis (Freely Movable Joints): These joints permit a wide range of movements, such as flexion, adduction, and pronation. Only synovial joints fall into this category. They are further divided into six types: Ball and socket joints (e.g., shoulder, hip) Hinge joints (e.g., elbow) Pivot joints (e.g., radius and ulna) Condyloid joints (e.g., wrist, knee) Saddle joints (e.g., thumb joint) Gliding joints (e.g., between carpals) Biomechanical Classification of Joints: Joints can also be classified based on their anatomical structure or biomechanical properties: 1. Simple Joints: These involve two articulating surfaces, such as the shoulder or hip joint. 2. Compound Joints: These involve three or more articulating surfaces, such as the radiocarpal joint. 3. Complex Joints: These involve three or more articulating surfaces and include an articular disc, such as the knee joint.
